content: The conventional method for smoking cessation typically involves quitting abruptly on a predetermined quit day. However, many individuals who smoke have made multiple unsuccessful attempts to quit and may prefer alternative strategies. One such alternative is reducing smoking gradually before quitting entirely. Before endorsing this approach, it is essential to determine whether gradual reduction is as effective as abrupt cessation and to explore ways to optimize reduction strategies to improve cessation outcomes. The objective of this research was to evaluate the impact of reduction-to-quit interventions on long-term smoking cessation. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO, using terms such as cold turkey, gradual, taper, and smoking reduction. The search also included trial registries to identify unpublished studies, with the most recent search conducted on October 29, 2018. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) where participants were advised to reduce smoking before quitting entirely. This advice could be delivered through self-help materials or behavioral support, with or without pharmacotherapy. Studies were excluded if they did not assess smoking cessation as an outcome, had follow-up periods of less than six months, involved spontaneous reduction without advice, aimed for reduction without cessation, or focused on switching to low-nicotine cigarettes without reducing smoking frequency or duration. Trials involving pregnant women were also excluded. Standard Cochrane methods were employed for data collection and analysis. Smoking cessation was assessed at least six months after intervention, using the most rigorous definitions available and analyzed on an intention-to-treat basis. Risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for cessation outcomes. Studies were grouped based on the type of comparison (e.g., no treatment, abrupt quitting, or other reduction-to-quit interventions), and meta-analyses were performed where appropriate using a Mantel-Haenszel random-effects model. Additional data on quit attempts, pre-quit smoking reduction, adverse events (AEs), serious adverse events (SAEs), and nicotine withdrawal symptoms were extracted and analyzed when sufficient data were available. A total of 51 trials involving 22,509 participants were included. Most participants were adults recruited from the community, typically smoking an average of 23 cigarettes per day. Eighteen studies were judged to have a high risk of bias, but restricting the analysis to studies with low or unclear risk of bias did not significantly alter the results. When comparing reduction-to-quit interventions with no treatment, the evidence was of very low certainty due to bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. The pooled analysis suggested a potential increase in cessation rates with reduction-to-quit interventions (RR 1.74, 95% CI 0.90 to 3.38; I² = 45%; 6 studies, 1,599 participants), but the results were inconclusive. When comparing reduction-to-quit interventions with abrupt quitting, the evidence indicated no significant difference in quit rates between the two approaches (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.17; I² = 29%; 22 studies, 9,219 participants). This estimate was judged to be of moderate certainty, limited by imprecision. Subgroup analysis suggested that reduction-to-quit interventions might be more effective than abrupt quitting when varenicline is used as a reduction aid (P = 0.01, I² = 77%). Additionally, when comparing reduction with pharmacotherapy to reduction without pharmacotherapy, low-certainty evidence indicated that pharmacotherapy-assisted reduction resulted in higher quit rates (RR 1.68, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.58; I² = 78%; 11 studies, 8,636 participants). However, subgroup analysis (P < 0.001, I² = 80% for subgroup differences) suggested that this effect was primarily observed with fast-acting nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) or varenicline (both moderate-certainty evidence), but not with nicotine patches, combination NRT, or bupropion (all lowor very low-certainty evidence). Further research is likely to alter the interpretation of these findings. Behavioral support for reduction-to-quit interventions appeared to result in higher quit rates compared to self-help resources alone. However, comparisons of other characteristics of reduction-to-quit interventions did not provide clear evidence of enhanced efficacy. Adverse events, serious adverse events, and nicotine withdrawal symptoms were inconsistently and infrequently reported across studies. There was some evidence that adverse events were more common in studies involving pharmacotherapy-assisted reduction compared to no pharmacotherapy, but these events were generally mild and consistent with typical NRT side effects. There was no clear evidence of differences in serious adverse events or withdrawal symptoms between trial arms. In conclusion, moderate-certainty evidence suggests that neither reduction-to-quit nor abrupt quitting interventions are superior in achieving long-term smoking cessation. Evidence comparing reduction-to-quit interventions with no treatment was inconclusive and of low certainty. Low-certainty evidence indicates that reduction-to-quit interventions may be more effective when pharmacotherapy, particularly fast-acting NRT or varenicline, is used as an aid. Data on adverse effects were sparse, but no significant increase in serious adverse events or withdrawal symptoms was observed. Future research should focus on isolating the effects of reduction strategies and identifying the most effective components of reduction-to-quit interventions to maximize cessation rates.
